description: 35th Annual FIRST Conference talks from 35th Annual FIRST Conference 2023.

talks.title: FIRST Hall of Fame Remarks & Mid-week Updates
talks.teaser: A midweek session blends conference logistics, CTF leaderboard standings, and tribute to a Hall of Fame inductee in incident response.
talks.summary:
The session opens with practical conference housekeeping: session surveys, the 2024 meeting in Fukuoka, program committee lunch details, the evening social, guest badge pickup, and hotel luggage storage for Friday departures. The speaker also promotes the Open Cyber Security Conference in Tenerife, planned for late February, as a one-off European event marking three decades of information sharing and incident response, run jointly by FIRST and the Open CSIRT Foundation.

David from the capture-the-flag organizers gives a midweek scoreboard update. Ten teams compete closely; reaching two thousand points earns a coin, and the leading team even captured every flag on the first day. He cites totals for released challenges, active players, per-user contributions, and notes that twenty additional flags went live that day, with a final batch planned before Friday’s winner announcement.

Board member Yuka outlines the Incident Response Hall of Fame, inaugurated in 2019 to honor long-term volunteer contributions to the response community. For 2023 the committee inducts Andrew Comack, who had recently died shortly before his sixtieth birthday. Colleagues Serge and Don recall his path from mathematics and early university networking roles through UK research networking leadership, TRANSITS training, ethics guidance work, and legal study that helped shape GDPR recital 49 for security-related data sharing. They emphasize his listening, mentorship, friendships, and how learning of the honor shortly before his death mattered to him, his wife Janet, and the wider FIRST community.

talks.title: UMQ? What Comes After TLP
talks.teaser: Explains why traffic light protocol falls short and surveys newer approaches for granular, machine-readable sharing rules.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how organisations share sensitive threat information and where the traffic light protocol (TLP) falls short. The speaker traces its origins to a US government response team that struggled to get restricted material used, and to the later standardisation and revision of the protocol. TLP only states how far material may be passed on, leaving open questions about encryption, permitted actions and licensing.

The speaker reviews other approaches being tried. ACS is a lengthy US government specification that depends on strong legal policies already being in place. PAP is used by some response teams, but its colours match TLP's, which could confuse newcomers, and each colour tries to answer two questions at once. IEP answers handling and action questions in granular, discrete ways, but leans on JSON blobs that are awkward to attach to the PDFs that still carry most guidance. The speaker argues for answers that people can read first and machines can parse second.

In the question round, attendees asked whether metadata could ride inside PDF files and how granular guidance can get before people lose track of it under time pressure. Another asked whether non-technical actions, such as shaping policy, belong in the definitions, and a UK participant described using permitted-action settings to guide government policy staff. The speaker closed by urging attendees to join a birds-of-a-feather session and to apply TLP when material leaves an organisation.

talks.title: Sliding Down the Slippery Analogy Slope and Landing in Clarity
talks.teaser: Shows how security analogies from law, war and medicine can mislead audiences, and how to communicate more precisely.
talks.summary:
Gene Spafford, co-author of a book on cybersecurity myths and miscommunications, argues that the analogies people use to explain the field often mislead. Because there is no single agreed definition of cybersecurity, one term can mean different things to engineers, lawyers, managers, regulators and the public.

He gives several examples. To a lawyer, saying data was stolen implies the owner lost its use, whereas practitioners treat copying and destruction as separate harms. Military phrases such as cyber Pearl Harbor or cyber 911 are largely U.S.-centric and carry different weight in other countries. A castle-and-moat picture suggests attackers can be seen coming and leaves out supply chain issues and insider threats. Lock-and-key comparisons for encryption have fed policy demands for key access that the technology does not support, and medical words like virus, worm and bacteria confused journalists and the public in the early days of malware.

He closes with practical advice. Know what your audience already understands, including their native language, state nuance explicitly instead of implying it, and remember that advisories and guidance get quoted, so the wording should be right the first time. Use analogies to clarify a precise term after introducing it, not to replace it. In questions, he noted that firewall has come to describe far more than its original meaning and pointed to NIST, ISO and IEEE, which publish differing definitions.

talks.title: Annual General Meeting (AGM) and FIRST Update / Q&A
talks.teaser: Covers FIRST's annual general meeting, the board election and bylaws vote, and the year's membership, finance and program updates.
talks.summary:
This session opened with the annual general meeting, covering quorum and the outcome of the board elections. Quorum was reached with 267 proxies, about 40 percent of the 665 eligible voting members. Seven candidates stood for the board, and a bylaws update passed with 208 votes in favour, 47 abstentions and 12 against. The outgoing board members were thanked, and the new board was to be confirmed at its meeting that day.

The members update followed, covering the year's organisational work. Membership stood at 679 full members and 127 liaison members, with 70 new teams joining since the previous AGM and 26 teams dropped. Membership had doubled over the last six years, and members now come from 105 countries. Reports covered the membership committee, the annual report, a diversity and inclusion statement, and infrastructure work, including a migration of on-premise systems to AWS. The finance overview showed revenue of around 3.2 million US dollars against expenses of around 3.5 million, a planned negative change in net assets, and a move toward full cost accounting for activities.

Further updates covered policy engagement at the United Nations, new memoranda with partners, the events calendar, the education and training program, the Fellowship program with 21 teams, and the special interest groups. The session closed with a question and answer period, during which no questions were raised from the floor.

talks.title: Keynote: Why Gender Diversity is Better Security
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Why Gender Diversity is Better Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote address at a FIRST conference, speakers Allison Pytlak and Nina Kollars explore why gender diversity is essential to building more effective cybersecurity defenses. Emphasizing that gender diversity is an issue that affects everyone rather than women alone, the speakers share personal experiences from diplomacy, the Department of Defense, and the hacker community. They examine how narrow thinking creates systemic security vulnerabilities, why addressing the shortage of cyber defenders requires broadening representation, and how organizations can actively dismantle cultural and architectural barriers to build more resilient teams.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Gender Diversity and Stereotypes**: Diversity encompasses women, men, non-binary individuals, and sexual orientations, intersecting with race, age, and class. The speakers contrast equal numerical representation with fair representation, noting how unexamined stereotypes undermine equity.
- **Feminist Curiosity and Gender Analysis**: Borrowing Cynthia Enloe's concept of 'feminist curiosity', the speakers urge practitioners to ask fundamental questions about who holds resources, who is heard, and what power dynamics exist in technical and policy spaces.
- **Cognitive Energy and Cultural Architecture**: Dr. Kollars recounts experiences within deeply gendered environments, such as a bilateral naval exchange in China and Department of Defense meetings, highlighting the disproportionate cognitive and emotional strain required to navigate spaces where one is presumed not to belong.
- **Imposter Syndrome and Technical Gatekeeping**: Gatekeeping language around who is considered 'technical' harms practitioners; anyone analyzing technology and its social implications should own their technical identity.
- **Narrow Security Perspectives as Vulnerabilities**: Failure to evaluate systems through a gendered lens creates blind spots. Real-world examples include dating apps being weaponized by authorities in homophobic regimes to entrap individuals, doctored sexually explicit images weaponized against women parliamentarians, and internet shutdowns disproportionately hurting women-owned businesses in informal economies.
- **Workforce Shortages and Representation Gaps**: There is a persistent deficit of cyber defenders. Yet, computer science degrees awarded to women in the U.S. dropped from 27% in 1997 to 19% in 2016, compounded by significant median salary disparities ($66,000 for women versus $90,000 for men).

### Technical Details & Real-World Examples
- **Weaponization of Consumer Apps**: Consumer platforms designed with benign intentions often introduce critical threat vectors when deployed in hostile socio-political environments, such as location-based dating applications repurposed by state police to track, arrest, or perpetrate physical violence against queer populations.
- **Disinformation and Online Abuse**: Research cited from the Inter-Parliamentary Union found that among surveyed women parliamentarians across 39 countries, 81.8% experienced psychological violence online, with 41.8% exposed to humiliating or sexually explicit doctored imagery, directly threatening participation in public governance.
- **Economic Impact of Network Disruptions**: Analysis of state-imposed internet blackouts revealed that women suffered disproportionate disruption when relying heavily on mobile-first apps like Instagram for informal commerce, where over 64% of affected micro-businesses were female-owned.

### Takeaways
- **Proactive Management and Workplace Design**: Leaders must anticipate needs (e.g., dedicated lactation rooms, family-friendly scheduling, accessible spaces for neurodivergent or differently abled colleagues) before workplaces become accidentally hostile.
- **Horizontal Sponsorship**: Peer-level support, advocating for junior talent, and deliberately sponsoring underrepresented colleagues into career openings creates sustained pathways for retention.
- **Normalize Support Communities**: Building external peer groups, mentorship channels, and safe sounding boards helps practitioners withstand the energy toll of navigating heavily male-dominated technical environments.

talks.title: An Introduction to EPSS, The Exploit Prediction Scoring System
talks.teaser: Introduces the Exploit Prediction Scoring System, which estimates how likely each vulnerability is to be exploited.
talks.summary:
This introductory talk presents the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS), a free model that estimates the chance a given vulnerability will be exploited in the wild within the next 30 days. The speakers start from the vulnerability management problem. With more than 200,000 known vulnerabilities and only a small share, often estimated at a few percent, ever exploited, patching by severity alone is inefficient. They point out that CVSS severity has little meaningful correlation with actual exploitation, so teams that patch high-severity findings first spend much of their effort on flaws attackers never use.

EPSS is built from observed exploitation data contributed by partner organisations, combined with other features of each vulnerability. Scores can be downloaded as a CSV file or pulled through an API. Because the outputs are true probabilities, they can be combined to estimate risk for a single server, a subnet or a whole enterprise. Since raw scores are often tiny, the model also provides a rank percentile that makes ordering easier to grasp. The presenters walk through exploitation trends, noting that attempted exploitation rises sharply in the first year after disclosure, and that a large share of exploited vulnerabilities are more than five years old, with about a third older than ten.

The speakers are candid about limits. The data comes mainly from public internet sensors, so IoT, automotive and medical device issues are poorly covered, and a missing exploitation signal does not prove a flaw is safe. Attendees are invited to try the scores, share exploitation observations that need only a CVE ID and a date, or join the EPSS special interest group.

talks.title: Five Easy Ways to Spoof Contributor/Package Reputation
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers fake package stars, repo history and contributor profiles so malicious open source code looks trustworthy.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why developers trust open source packages based on surface signals such as popularity, stars and contributor profiles. The speaker's research team analyses packages from public registries by checking their behaviour, contributor history and threat intelligence. Several campaigns are described: a typosquatted package that downloaded its payload from a GitHub repository and used it as a command channel, switching to new account names when blocked; a package that installed a malicious browser extension to swap copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses; and a package that hid code inside an image and used a Discord channel as its command server.

Tracking the actors behind these packages led to registry accounts that were prepared in advance and used in batches. The team used sitemap files to enumerate user accounts and block dormant ones, then mapped hundreds of related packages to a threat actor group that distributed backdoored tools to newcomers. In a live shell demonstration, researchers relayed their own messages into an attacker's command session.

The core of the talk covers five ways to spoof reputation. Star jacking links a malicious package to a legitimate repository so the registry copies its stars. Repo jacking exploits renamed GitHub accounts whose old URLs still redirect to names an attacker can reclaim. Fake commits with altered timestamps build a false history, fake contributors can be attached to a project, and organization names are free text, so a fake company can appear verified. A bonus route is simply asking a maintainer for access. The takeaway is that stars, popularity and profiles are not evidence of safety.

talks.title: The Female Conversation: Empowering Female Talent in Incident Response
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Female Conversation: Empowering Female Talent in Incident Response.
talks.summary:
Overview:
A panel of cybersecurity leaders convened at the FIRST conference to address the underrepresentation of women in Incident Response (IR) and Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI). Led by Rebecca Taylor of Secureworks, the session brings together operational experts from VMware, Juniper Networks, Richemont, and Carnegie Mellon's CERT Division. The discussion examines actionable organizational frameworks to hire, retain, and develop female professionals, offering practical solutions to dismantle barriers within technical cybersecurity operations.

Key Topics:
- Industry diversity metrics: (ISC)² reports of 24% female workforce representation and Microsoft survey data on perceived career complexity
- Re-engineering recruitment practices: Outcome-based job descriptions versus exhaustive technical qualification checklists
- Mitigating gendered linguistic bias in technical cybersecurity role postings (e.g., "ninja", "dominant")
- Expanding STEM talent pipelines beyond traditional university programs into early childhood education

Technical Details:
The panel opens by benchmarking industry diversity statistics against operational reality. According to studies by (ISC)², women constitute approximately 24% of the global cybersecurity workforce, while wider digital workforce participation has stagnated at roughly 17% over the past decade according to The Guardian. Furthermore, research conducted by Microsoft revealed that 71% of surveyed women perceive cybersecurity as too complex a career path, and 27% believe men are viewed as a better cultural fit for security roles. While corporate initiatives—such as Secureworks CEO Wendy Thomas targeting 50% female global representation by 2030—demonstrate executive intent, practical execution requires structural shifts in operational recruitment and retention.

The panelists focus on the recruitment process as a primary bottleneck. Emma O'Neill highlights research indicating that while men frequently apply for positions when meeting roughly 50% of listed qualifications, female candidates typically apply only when fulfilling nearly all stated criteria. Traditional job postings that feature exhaustive laundry lists of technical requirements and certifications inadvertently exclude capable non-traditional talent. To solve this, organizations must restructure job specifications around role outcomes—defining what daily success looks like and how transferable skills apply—rather than maintaining rigid prerequisite checklists.

Additionally, the panel examines the role of linguistic bias in technical recruitment. Job postings frequently incorporate aggressive or masculine jargon—such as demanding "ninja engineers" or "dominant leadership"—which subtly signals exclusionary workplace cultures. Panelists also address pipeline development, noting that corporate outreach concentrated exclusively at the university level or late secondary school (ages 12-15) occurs too late to influence educational trajectories. Effective long-term talent acquisition requires industry engagement in primary education, demystifying technology concepts before societal stereotypes take root.

Key Takeaways:
Recruiting organizations should replace exhaustive certification checklists with outcome-oriented job postings that articulate daily responsibilities and success criteria. Hiring managers must audit job descriptions to remove exclusionary, gendered language like "ninja" that discourages diverse applicants. Building a sustainable talent pipeline requires organizations to invest in STEM outreach at early developmental stages rather than relying solely on university-level recruiting.

talks.title: Mistakes Happen, Either Learn From Them Or Rinse And Repeat!
talks.teaser: Shows common incident response mistakes from a CSIRT's ransomware cases and the practical fixes that came from them.
talks.summary:
Gregor Wegberg, who leads digital forensics and incident response at the Oneconsult CSIRT, looks at mistakes his team has made during everyday ransomware and intrusion cases. He argues that the technical side is already well covered, while the harder problems are people, process and communication.

A case involving an IT provider to hospitals shows how a sign reading "war room" on the door got management to approve containment steps they had previously resisted. The team's monthly lessons-learned meeting was set for Friday afternoons, and no session has yet had more than half the team attending. On site, customers often freeze, or IT staff change domain admin settings and firewall rules without keeping records. In one case, admins used domain administrator accounts on every device, which let attackers run Mimikatz. The speaker himself went three days on about two hours of sleep and made poor decisions nobody flagged, so incident leads should make sure people eat, drink and rest.

Practical takeaways include planning the first 12 hours, including who works when; telling management that only about half the staff will be available and working at reduced efficiency; avoiding blame mid-incident; asking why each system is being restored; tracking tasks on paper, flip charts or kanban boards; and writing small, modular playbooks, such as one for the first hour and one for credential resets.

talks.title: Objectifying Your Incident Management to Lift the Fog of IR
talks.teaser: Shows how to frame incident objectives, workstreams and confidence levels so stakeholders get clear updates during crises.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how incident responders can organise communication with executives and other stakeholders during major crises, when briefings often trigger a flood of questions. The speaker explains that senior audiences are experts who weigh six or seven criteria in a non-linear way, so leading with the most decisive items, and showing evidence rather than gaps, lets them decide quickly.

The speaker builds an incident view step by step. Objectives are written to SMART-style attributes, for example identifying exfiltrated data from a database before a set date. Each objective is split into tasks grouped into workstreams, each with a lead, members and key activities. Each task records current and future confidence (low, moderate or high), a time estimate, progress and notes. A data breach example shows how learning whether data was public or sensitive can reorder priorities, and why a task that cannot improve should be decided on rather than waited for. Gold, silver and bronze tiers, drawn from firefighting and tied to NIST and FEMA guidance, set the briefing cadence.

In questions, the speaker suggested that stakeholders who reject bad news often need facts, metrics and trusted outside opinions first, and that technical staff should not necessarily join executive meetings. A live, shared view lets executives check progress on their own, turning updates into short conversations rather than repeated status requests.

talks.title: No One Likes to be Excluded: What Is the Role of War Exclusions in Cyber Insurance?
talks.teaser: Panelists dissect Lloyd's cyber war exclusions and why state attribution makes them hard to apply.
talks.summary:
A panel at the FIRST conference examined war exclusions in cyber insurance and what they mean for incident response. The moderator traced war exclusions back to the 1700s, when insurers ruled out war losses that could exceed the capital available to pay them. Terrorism exclusions after 9/11 followed the same logic, and the panelists argued that attributing a cyber operation to a state is harder still.

The panel went through the Lloyd's Market Association cyber exclusions, which come in four versions with A and B variants. Several versions would deny or limit payment when a cyber operation is attributed to a state. Panelists pointed out that state actors can use commodity malware, that a recent court ruling on a 1.4 billion claim under a property policy showed the wording was unclear, and that an insurer paid out after the Anthem breach without any attribution or forensic work. A Hong Kong example showed a company using its cyber insurance to get investigation and legal support after data theft, while a speaker from Ghana said limited attribution capability in African markets would shape how the clauses are applied.

The main takeaways were that insurers and incident responders need far more dialogue, that underwriting should judge process maturity rather than surface checks such as open ports, and that the industry lacks shared evidence on which controls actually reduce incidents. Buyers were encouraged to read exclusions closely and decide which ones they will accept.

talks.title: You Are a Manager Harry
talks.teaser: Draws lessons from a team leader's move from incident response into managing a DevSecOps team.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads a 12-person DevSecOps team at a security team serving European institutions and agencies, traces a career path from penetration testing through threat intelligence, digital forensics and incident response, and detection engineering. They describe how each role shaped their expectations, and how a hacker's habit of writing quick, working-first scripts ran into reality when the people who wrote them left and the scripts broke without documentation.

Several cases illustrate friction between teams. Two groups built the same log-gap detection without knowing about each other, which the speaker says cost about three weeks of duplicated effort. Staff from different teams also misunderstood each other's work, so the speaker's team started short internal sessions where anyone can present a technique. An SSO rollout was redesigned once the group realised it would become a single point of failure, and the team now brings offensive-minded people into project design to question what a new service would expose.

The main takeaway is that moving into management meant accepting that colleagues would do work their own way and resisting micromanagement. The speaker also stresses planning over rushed projects, standardising how projects are tracked, and raising security questions early in design. In the Q&A, the speaker notes that duplicated work can sometimes produce a better result, but that overlapping projects strain teams that are already overloaded.

talks.title: ISO 27035 Practical Value for CSIRTs and SOCs
talks.teaser: Assesses the ISO/IEC 27035 incident management standard and tests its definitions and guidance against real CSIRT and SOC practice.
talks.summary:
This FIRST conference talk examines ISO/IEC 27035, the multi-part standard on information security incident management, and asks whether it helps the CSIRTs and SOCs expected to follow it. The speaker is a practitioner of incident management rather than a user of the standard. Three parts are published and a fourth, covering coordination, is still in development. The text is aimed at internal teams and expands on the ISO 27001 controls for incident handling.

The middle of the talk compares the standard's model with how detection and incident work runs day to day. The speaker finds the definitions hard to apply: an information security event becomes an incident only when there is risk of harm, and the incident response team and incident management team roles blur together. Vulnerabilities are treated as events without a matching report type. The parts also use different incident categories, one offering a classification in an appendix and another listing different types in its reporting template. Phrases such as detecting and reporting "as soon as possible" are vague, and a requirement that event reports contain every fact would stall a busy team. Mapped onto a services model, change management and threat intelligence had no clear home.

The closing argument is that the standard offers structure but thin substance. It suits organisations building their security operations top-down from ISO 27001, especially in heavily regulated settings. Teams that set their own objectives first may find it constraining. The speaker suggests drawing on established services models for workflow and ownership detail, and favours pragmatic processes that use limited resources well. In the discussion, an audience member said some organisations already use the standard, and the speaker concluded that its value depends on how well a team fills the gaps.

talks.title: Using Apple Sysdiagnose for Forensics and Integrity Check
talks.teaser: Shows how Apple sysdiagnose archives can support iPhone forensics and integrity checks without jailbreaking the device.
talks.summary:
Forensic examiners often need to check the state of an Apple device without jailbreaking it and while collecting as little user data as possible. This talk looks at sysdiagnose, a diagnostic bundle that Apple devices can generate for debugging. It holds process information, battery and memory data, network configuration, Wi-Fi history and system logs, but usually not personal content such as messages or photos. The speakers compared it with the Mobile Verification Toolkit, which depends on user backups, and argued that the two approaches are complementary.

The presenters described an open-source, modular framework that converts the mixed output of a sysdiagnose archive, with its many file types and timestamp formats, into standardised JSON. It includes 25 parsers, each of which can run on its own, and four analyzers. One analyzer sends time-based data to Timesketch for timeline review, two produce KML or GPX maps of Wi-Fi networks seen by the device, and one builds a list of application identifiers to help spot rogue apps. Live demos showed a Wi-Fi network from the device history placed on a map, an app installed during a handover appearing in a timeline, and a reverse shell process found in the process logs.

The speakers were candid about limitations. The collection runs standard binaries on the device, so malware with operating-system-level access could affect the results, meaning the output is not fully forensically sound. Apple also changes file formats between major iOS releases, which breaks parsers and regular expressions and requires ongoing maintenance. They invited feedback, new parsers and sample archives from analysts.

talks.title: Assessing e-Government DNS Resilience
talks.teaser: A multi-country study measures authoritative DNS for government domains and outlines redundancy gaps, anycast use, and hardening steps.
talks.summary:
Researchers from the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre, university partners, and SIDN Labs examined how electronic government domains depend on authoritative DNS when citizens need digital services to stay online. The talk opens with wartime monitoring that showed prolonged resolution failures for a Russian domain whose three name servers were unicast but shared one hosting prefix, and with TransIP incidents in the Netherlands that stretched resolution times and caused widespread lookup failures.

The study compared government domain lists from the Netherlands, Switzerland, Sweden, and the United States. The team mapped name server records, IPv4 and IPv6 placement, autonomous system diversity, anycast adoption, TTL values, and top mail providers. Roughly two in five domains relied on a single authoritative DNS operator; U.S. dot gov domains often had one provider but frequently mitigated risk with anycast. Provider concentration appeared in every country, including cloud-hosted Swedish cases and Swiss domains that clustered on shared network prefixes with weak IPv6 spread. Short caching hints on name server records increased query load compared with longer recommended values.

Practical takeaways stress geographic and network diversity for secondary DNS, sensible TTL planning with care during DNSSEC changes, and wider anycast deployment. For decentralized governments that outsource hosting, a central anycast secondary name server could add robustness with minimal zone changes. Most guidance applies to any organization running business-critical DNS, not only the public sector.
